paragraphs.text: See Psa 31:1, {see Trapp on "Psa 31:1"} It appeareth by Psa 71:9; Psa 71:18, that this psalm was written by David in his old age, when Absalom or Sheba was in rebellion against him, though haply for haste, and in that fright he could not superscribe it as he did the rest. The Greek title, viz. of David, a psalm of the sons of Jonadab, and of them that were first captived, hath no footing in the original Hebrew.
paragraphs.anchor: In thee, O Lord, do I put my trust

paragraphs.text: Let my deliverance be the fruit of thy promise and of my prayer; and so it will be much the sweeter.
paragraphs.anchor: Deliver me in thy righteousness

paragraphs.text: sc. To thine angels, and all other thy creatures; or, thou hast commanded, that is, thou hast promised.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast given commandment

paragraphs.text: That seeketh by fraud to undermine me, and by force to overturn me.
paragraphs.anchor: Out of the hand of the unrighteous

paragraphs.text: Qui totus in fermento iacet; sour as leaven, sharp as vinegar.
paragraphs.anchor: And cruel man

paragraphs.text: Helpless I may seem, but hopeless I am not.
paragraphs.anchor: For thou art my hope

paragraphs.text: As in the womb I lived upon thee, so from the womb. The same that breedeth us feedeth us; that matter that nourisheth the child in the womb striking up into the breasts, and by a further concoction becoming white, is made milk for it.
paragraphs.anchor: By thee have I been holden up from the womb

paragraphs.text: Thou art he that took me out of my mother’s bowels] Else I had never been born alive. That a child is born, fieri videmus, saith Galen, sed quomodo fiat, admirari tantum possumus. Avicenna calleth it, Opus supra mirabilia omnia mirabile, the greatest wonder in the world. Surely, if a child were born but once in a hundred years’ time, we should all run to see so strange a work, saith another.

Or, unto the great ones, a monster to the mighty, quia credo quod non video, as Austin glosseth, because I believe what I yet see not, viz. that this storm shall blow over, and I be resettled in my throne.
paragraphs.anchor: I am a wonder unto many

paragraphs.text: Minister unto me still fresh matter for my spirit to work upon.
paragraphs.anchor: Let my mouth be filled with thy praise

paragraphs.text: For now I have most need of thee. The white rose is soonest cankered, so is the white head soonest corrupted.
paragraphs.anchor: Cast me not off in the time of old age

paragraphs.text: Saepe nigrum cor est, caput album -

Satan maketh a prey of old Solomon, Asa, Lot, others; whom when young he could never so deceive. The heathens, therefore, well warn us to look well to our old age, as that which cometh not alone, but is infested with many diseases both of body and mind. This David knew, and therefore prayed, as here, "Cast me not off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength faileth." He is a rare old man that can say with Caleb, Jos 14:10-11. Omnia fert aetas, animum quoque.
Who, rather than their lives, would bereave me of mine; these would double murder me, first by detraction, and then by deadly practice.
paragraphs.anchor: For mine enemies

paragraphs.text: For his late sin against Uriah; and as may appear by his present distress, his forlorn proscribed condition.
paragraphs.anchor: God hath forsaken him

paragraphs.text: The insolence of his enemies sets an edge upon his prayers Oratio sine malis est avis sine alis. Our Saviour in his agony prayed the more earnestly, Luk 22:44.
paragraphs.anchor: O God, be not far from me

paragraphs.text: Here he beginneth diris devovere, to devote his foes to destruction, who soon also found that these were not bruta fulmina, as the pope’s bulls are (wittily compared by one to a fool’s dagger, rattling and snapping without an edge), but that there was an energy in them, though haply not felt for present; and that they had better have angered all the witches in the country than occasioned David thus to curse them in the name of the Lord.
paragraphs.anchor: Let them be confounded and consumed

paragraphs.text: I will lengthen out mine hope, as a line drawn out. Tremellius renders it, I am in expectation still of completing thy praise, and will go on therein, viz. when thou shalt have completed my deliverance
paragraphs.anchor: But I will hope continually

paragraphs.text: Lo, here, a sweet and comfortable conjunction of God’s righteousness and our salvation. See 2Th 1:6-7.
paragraphs.anchor: My mouth shall show forth thy righteousness and thy salvation

paragraphs.text: Or, though I know not, &c., by a modest correction, since they may be celebrated, but not enumerated.
paragraphs.anchor: For I know not the numbers thereof

paragraphs.text: Littora quot conchas, quot amaena rosaria flores,
Quotve soporiferum grana papaver habet:
Sylva feras quot alit, quot piscibus unda natatur,
Et tenerum pennis acra pulsar avis (Ovid.).
So many, and ten thousand times more, are God’s lovingkindnesses. The psalmist elsewhere venteth himself by an exclamation, Psa 31:19. {See Trapp on "Psa 31:19"}

Ingrediar in potentia Domini, I will do what I can, with God’s help, in glorifying his name, though I cannot do as I would and as I ought; Narrabo res inenarrabiles, and then entreat those that hear me to think higher things of God than I am able to utter.
paragraphs.anchor: I will go in the strength of the Lord God

paragraphs.text: For that is enough, and more than I can well do; I will not once mention (as profane persons use to do) mine own wisdom, valour, &c.; alas, they are not worthy to be named in the same day with thine.
paragraphs.anchor: Even of thine only

paragraphs.text: Happy David in such a school master. All the faithful are taught of God; outwardly by his word and works, inwardly by his Spirit: Et quando Christus magister quam cito discitur quod docetur? Nescit tarda molimina Spiritus Sancti gratia (Aug. Ambrose).
paragraphs.anchor: O God, thou hast taught me

paragraphs.text: Now, that the plum tree is full of blooms, the map of age is figured in my forehead, the calendar of death appeareth in the furrows of my face; let me do nothing to spot my white head. Let me, with the sun, give greatest glimpse at the going down, and, with the rose, retain my sweetness, though I have lost my colour. See Psa 71:9.
paragraphs.anchor: Now also when I am old and gray headed

paragraphs.text: Mirus fervor Davidis in celebranda bonitate Dei, saith Vatablus here. David would propagate God’s praise to all posterity.
paragraphs.anchor: And thy power to every one that is to come

paragraphs.text: Far above the reach of human reason; yet for the strengthening of my hope, I will look up after it, though mine eye should be tired in the way.
paragraphs.anchor: Thy righteousness also, O God, is very high

paragraphs.text: Angustias magnas et malas, and hast thereby taught me, Psa 71:17, Quae nocent, docent.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou which hast showed me great and sore troubles

paragraphs.text: And this is one singular height of thy righteousness, that thou carriest tby people through so many deaths, and causest them to ascend from the lowest ebb of affliction to the highest pitch of comfort. Stoics ascribe such occurrences to fate, epicures to fortune, but David to God alone.
paragraphs.anchor: Shall quicken me again

paragraphs.text: Meam, id est Tuam, quam mihi dedisti, saith the Arabic gloss here; my greatness, that is, thy greatness which thou hast given me.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou shall increase my greatness

paragraphs.text: In organo natali, with an instrument made like a bottle.
paragraphs.anchor: I will also praise thee with the psaltery

paragraphs.text: Who sanctifiest thine throughout, and art to be sanctified of thine throughout all eternity, Isa 5:16.
paragraphs.anchor: O thou Holy One of Israel

paragraphs.text: Hearts and lips shall concur in this work. The voice which is made in the mouth is nothing so sweet as that which cometh from the depth of the breast. The deeper and hollower the belly of the lute or viol is, the pleasanter is the sound; the fleeter, the more grating and harsh in our ears.
paragraphs.anchor: And my soul, which thou hast redeemed

paragraphs.text: Advisedly talk, and upon due deliberation. What a mad edict was that of Henry II of France, that men should not talk at all of Scriptural matters! And that of the Jesuits at Dola, forbidding any talk of God, either in good sort or in bad!
paragraphs.anchor: My tongue also shall talk of thy righteousness
